note: Questions from the CBSE Class XII Biology board exam 2025, Q.P. code 57/1/1, published by CBSE at cbse.gov.in. Questions that depend on a diagram (Q7, Q23 and Q32(B)) are left out; other figures are described in words. Solutions are written for this portal and are not CBSE's official marking scheme.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A man whose father was colour-blind marries a woman who had a colour-blind mother and a normal father. What percentage of male children of this couple will be colour-blind?
questions.solution: The woman received an affected X from her mother, so she is a carrier. Sons get their X from the mother, so half the sons are colour-blind (the father's X does not pass to sons).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: GEAC stands for
questions.solution: The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Match Column A with Column B: (i) Lady bird beetle (ii) Mycorrhiza (iii) Biological control (iv) Biogas — (a) Methanobacterium (b) Trichoderma (c) Aphids (d) Glomus. Choose the correct option for (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) in order.
questions.solution: Lady bird beetles eat aphids; Glomus forms mycorrhiza; Trichoderma is a biocontrol fungus; Methanobacterium produces biogas.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The process of mineralisation by microorganisms helps in the release of :
options: both organic and inorganic nutrients from detritus.
inorganic nutrients from detritus and formation of humus.
questions.solution: Humus is degraded slowly by microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients (mineralisation).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Transplantation of tissues or organs often fails due to rejection by the body of the patient. Which type of immune response is responsible for such rejection?
questions.solution: Graft rejection is due to cell-mediated immunity (T-lymphocytes).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Match Column I with Column II: (a) Trophoblast (b) Implantation (c) Inner cell mass (d) Morula — (i) Embedding of blastocyst in the endometrium (ii) Group of cells that would differentiate as embryo (iii) Embryo with 8–16 blastomeres (iv) Outer layer of blastocyst. Choose the option for (a), (b), (c), (d) in order.
questions.solution: Trophoblast is the outer layer, implantation is embedding in the endometrium, the inner cell mass forms the embryo and the morula has 8-16 blastomeres.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Amplification of the gene of interest by using DNA polymerase (PCR) may go up to
questions.solution: Repeated PCR cycles can amplify a DNA segment about a billion times.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The sequence of bases in a segment of the coding strand of DNA is 5′-AATGCTAGGCAC-3′. Choose the correct sequence of bases in the mRNA transcribed from this DNA.
questions.solution: mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: How many pollen grains and ovules are likely to be formed in the anther and the ovary of an angiosperm bearing 50 microspore mother cells and 50 megaspore mother cells respectively?
questions.solution: Each microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen grains (200). Each ovule has one megaspore mother cell, so 50 ovules.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Choose the correct series of human evolution.
options: Dryopithecus → Homo erectus → Australopithecines → Homo sapiens
Australopithecines → Homo erectus → Neanderthal → Homo sapiens
Homo erectus → Australopithecines → Homo sapiens → Neanderthal
questions.solution: Australopithecines came first, then Homo erectus, then Neanderthal man, and finally Homo sapiens.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: RNA interference (RNAi) helps in making the tobacco plant resistant to a nematode (Meloidegyne incognitia). Choose the option that shows how RNAi is achieved :
options: Preventing the process of translation of mRNA of the nematode.
Preventing the process of replication of DNA of the nematode.
Preventing the process of transcription of DNA of the plant.
Preventing the process of replication of DNA of the plant.
questions.solution: dsRNA made in the plant silences the specific mRNA of the nematode, so it cannot be translated and the parasite dies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Saheli is the world's first non-steroidal oral contraceptive pill.
Reason (R): It has been developed by the National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution: Saheli, the once-a-week non-steroidal pill, was developed by CDRI, Lucknow, so R is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): One of the properties of the genetic code is degeneracy.
Reason (R): Some amino acids can be coded by more than one codon.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution: Degeneracy means one amino acid can have several codons, which is exactly what R says.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): A bioreactor provides the optimal conditions for achieving the desired product by providing optimum growth conditions.
Reason (R): The most commonly used bioreactors are of the stirring type.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution: Both are true, but the type of bioreactor does not explain why it gives optimum conditions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): When the two genes in a dihybrid cross are situated on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations is much higher than the non-parental type.
Reason (R): Higher parental gene combinations can be attributed to crossing over between the two genes.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution: Linkage keeps parental combinations together; crossing over produces recombinants, so R is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: How are morphine and heroin related? Mention their effect on the human body.
questions.solution: Heroin (smack) is diacetylmorphine, obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant (Papaver somniferum). Both are opioids that bind to opioid receptors in the CNS and gut; heroin is a depressant that slows down body functions, while morphine is a strong sedative and painkiller.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Name an alcoholic drink produced with the help of microbes (1) with distillation (2) without distillation. (ii) Explain how cyanobacteria can be used as bio-fertilisers.
questions.solution: (i)(1) Whisky, brandy or rum. (2) Wine or beer. (ii) Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria fix atmospheric nitrogen and add organic matter to the soil, increasing its fertility, especially in paddy fields.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Analyse the following ecosystems and discuss which will be more productive in terms of primary productivity : a young forest, a natural old forest, a shallow polluted lake.
questions.solution: The young forest: its rapidly growing plants have a high rate of photosynthesis and biomass build-up. An old forest is near equilibrium (most production is used in respiration), and a polluted lake has low productivity because pollution reduces light and producer growth (eutrophication can briefly raise it, but overall it is low).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Differentiate between net primary productivity and gross primary productivity in an ecosystem.
questions.solution: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total rate of production of organic matter by photosynthesis. Net primary productivity (NPP) is what remains after the producers' respiration losses: NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the biomass available to consumers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A cross between a couple: father 44 + XY, mother 44 + XX. Because of non-disjunction, the father produces gametes 22 + XY and 22 + O, and the mother produces normal 22 + X gametes. Offspring 1 comes from 22 + XY sperm with 22 + X egg, and offspring 2 from 22 + O sperm with 22 + X egg. Identify the abnormalities 1 and 2 and distinguish between them.
questions.solution: 1 is 44 + XXY: Klinefelter's syndrome, a sterile male with some feminine features (gynaecomastia) and tall stature. 2 is 44 + XO: Turner's syndrome, a sterile female with rudimentary ovaries, short stature and lack of secondary sexual characters.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A pedigree shows the inheritance of blood groups. Parents: father (1) blood group B, mother (2) blood group A. Their children: 4 (son, A), 5 (son, AB), 6 (daughter, B) and 7 (son, A). Son 4 marries woman 3 (blood group B); their children are 8 (daughter, O) and 9 (son, B). (a) Give the possible genotypes of individuals 1 and 2. (b) Which antigens will be present on the plasma membrane of the RBCs of individuals 5 and 8?
questions.solution: (a) Individual 4 (group A) has a group O child, so he is IᴬI⁰ and got I⁰ from a parent. So 1 is IᴮI⁰ or IᴮIᴮ and 2 is IᴬI⁰ or IᴬIᴬ, with at least one of them heterozygous (carrying I⁰). (b) 5 (AB) has both A and B antigens; 8 (O) has neither.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A patient with ADA deficiency requires periodic infusion of genetically engineered lymphocytes. Explain why such periodic infusion is required and suggest a permanent cure for ADA deficiency.
questions.solution: The infused lymphocytes (carrying a functional ADA gene) are not immortal, so they die and must be replaced periodically. A permanent cure is introducing the ADA gene (isolated from marrow cells) into cells at an early embryonic stage, or into bone marrow stem cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Describe in brief any two techniques that can be used to transfer recombinant DNA into the host cell directly without using any vector.
questions.solution: Microinjection: recombinant DNA is injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell. Biolistics (gene gun): cells, especially plant cells, are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA. (Also: making bacterial cells competent with Ca²⁺ and heat shock.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Write the palindromic nucleotide sequence for the DNA segment 5′-GAATTC-3′. (b) Name the restriction endonuclease that recognises this sequence. (c) How are sticky ends produced? Mention their role.
questions.solution: (a) 5′-GAATTC-3′ / 3′-CTTAAG-5′ (both strands read the same 5′→3′). (b) EcoRI. (c) EcoRI cuts each strand between G and A, a little away from the centre of the palindrome, leaving single-stranded overhangs. These sticky ends form hydrogen bonds with complementary cut ends, which DNA ligase then joins, helping make recombinant DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Indiscriminate human activities such as alien species invasion, fragmentation and habitat loss have accelerated the loss of biodiversity. Justify by taking one example for each. (b) State the importance of (i) the IUCN Red Data List (ii) hot spots in conservation of biodiversity.
questions.solution: (a) Alien species: Nile perch in Lake Victoria wiped out over 200 cichlid fish species (or Parthenium, Lantana, water hyacinth, African catfish). Fragmentation: large animals and migratory birds needing large territories decline when forests are broken up. Habitat loss: clearing of tropical rain forests (e.g. Amazon) has destroyed habitats of many species. (b)(i) It documents species threatened with extinction and their status, guiding conservation priorities. (ii) Hotspots are regions of very high species richness and endemism under threat; protecting them can reduce ongoing extinctions greatly.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A diagram shows a thread P coiled around a spherical bead Q made of protein, with a small protein clip holding the thread where it enters and leaves. (a) Identify the structure shown. (b) Identify the labels P and Q. (c) Write the nature of histone proteins. (d) Distinguish between euchromatin and heterochromatin.
questions.solution: (a) A nucleosome. (b) P is DNA; Q is the histone octamer. (c) Histones are positively charged (basic) proteins, rich in lysine and arginine. (d) Euchromatin is loosely packed, lightly stained and transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is densely packed, darkly stained and inactive.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Shyam and Radha are expecting their first child, with Radha in her second month of pregnancy with no complications. Shyam's family has a history of cystic fibrosis while Radha's family has a history of Down's syndrome. (a) Suggest and explain a way of testing if their baby is at risk of any genetic disorder. (b) If one or both abnormalities are present and pose a risk to the mother's health, mention one possible option for them to consider. Is that option safe for Radha at the current gestational age? Justify. (c) Under what conditions is the process in (b) illegal?
questions.solution: (a) Amniocentesis (or chorionic villus sampling): fetal cells from the amniotic fluid are cultured and their chromosomes and genes are analysed for disorders such as Down's syndrome and cystic fibrosis. (b) Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP); it is relatively safe in the first trimester (up to 12 weeks), and Radha is in her second month. (c) MTP is illegal when used for female foeticide (sex determination followed by abortion of a normal female foetus), or when done by unqualified persons or beyond the legal limits.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Explain the basis on which the gel electrophoresis technique works. Write any two ways the products obtained through this technique can be utilised.
questions.solution: DNA fragments are negatively charged, so in an electric field they move through an agarose gel matrix towards the anode; the gel sieves them, so smaller fragments move farther, separating them by size. Bands are seen after staining with ethidium bromide under UV light and cut out (elution). Uses: constructing recombinant DNA by joining the eluted fragments with cloning vectors; DNA fingerprinting; checking the products of restriction digestion or PCR.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Compare and contrast convergent and divergent evolution.
questions.solution: Divergent evolution: the same ancestral structure develops along different directions to suit different needs, giving homologous organs (e.g. forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human; Darwin's finches; adaptive radiation of marsupials). Convergent evolution: unrelated organisms independently evolve similar structures for similar functions, giving analogous organs (e.g. wings of butterfly and bird, eyes of octopus and mammals, flippers of penguins and dolphins). Both are driven by natural selection; divergent shows common ancestry, convergent shows similar habitats.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Two graphs show hormone levels through the menstrual cycle. Case 1: hormone P rises sharply to a peak in the middle of the cycle, just before ovulation, and then falls; hormone Q rises after ovulation in the luteal phase and then falls back. Case 2: hormone P shows the same mid-cycle peak, but hormone Q keeps rising through the luteal phase and does not fall, and hCG starts rising towards the end of the luteal phase.

Which hormone is responsible for the peak observed in Case 1 and Case 2? Write one function of that hormone.
questions.solution: LH (luteinising hormone): the LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and release of the ovum (ovulation).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Two graphs show hormone levels through the menstrual cycle. Case 1: hormone P rises sharply to a peak in the middle of the cycle, just before ovulation, and then falls; hormone Q rises after ovulation in the luteal phase and then falls back. Case 2: hormone P shows the same mid-cycle peak, but hormone Q keeps rising through the luteal phase and does not fall, and hCG starts rising towards the end of the luteal phase.

Write the changes that take place in the ovary and uterus during the follicular phase.
questions.solution: Ovary: primary follicles grow into a fully mature Graafian follicle under FSH and LH, and secrete oestrogen. Uterus: the endometrium regenerates and thickens through proliferation (proliferative phase).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Two graphs show hormone levels through the menstrual cycle. Case 1: hormone P rises sharply to a peak in the middle of the cycle, just before ovulation, and then falls; hormone Q rises after ovulation in the luteal phase and then falls back. Case 2: hormone P shows the same mid-cycle peak, but hormone Q keeps rising through the luteal phase and does not fall, and hCG starts rising towards the end of the luteal phase.

Name the hormone Q of Case 2. Write one function of hormone Q.
questions.solution: Progesterone: it maintains the endometrium, which is needed for implantation and continuation of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Two graphs show hormone levels through the menstrual cycle. Case 1: hormone P rises sharply to a peak in the middle of the cycle, just before ovulation, and then falls; hormone Q rises after ovulation in the luteal phase and then falls back. Case 2: hormone P shows the same mid-cycle peak, but hormone Q keeps rising through the luteal phase and does not fall, and hCG starts rising towards the end of the luteal phase.

Which structure in the ovary will remain functional in Case 2? How is it formed?
questions.solution: The corpus luteum; it forms from the remains of the ruptured Graafian follicle after ovulation, and is maintained by hCG when pregnancy occurs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
In nature, individuals of a species usually live in groups in a well-defined area, share or compete for similar resources, potentially interbreed and so form a population. A population has attributes that an individual does not, and is made up of individuals of different ages. Ecological processes such as competition, predation or the effect of pesticides are evaluated in terms of change in population size. Population size, technically called population density (N), need not be measured in numbers only, and it keeps changing with food availability, predation and weather.

The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator because of a special chemical in its body. How does the butterfly acquire this chemical?
questions.solution: During its caterpillar stage it feeds on a poisonous weed (milkweed) and stores the chemical in its body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
In nature, individuals of a species usually live in groups in a well-defined area, share or compete for similar resources, potentially interbreed and so form a population. A population has attributes that an individual does not, and is made up of individuals of different ages. Ecological processes such as competition, predation or the effect of pesticides are evaluated in terms of change in population size. Population size, technically called population density (N), need not be measured in numbers only, and it keeps changing with food availability, predation and weather.

If the population density at time t + 1 is 800, emigration = 100, immigration = 200, natality = 200 and mortality = 150, calculate the population density at time t and comment on the type of age pyramid that will be formed.
questions.solution: N(t+1) = N(t) + (B + I) − (D + E): 800 = N(t) + 400 − 250, so N(t) = 650. The population is growing, so the age pyramid is expanding (broad base, triangular).

questions.text:
In nature, individuals of a species usually live in groups in a well-defined area, share or compete for similar resources, potentially interbreed and so form a population. A population has attributes that an individual does not, and is made up of individuals of different ages. Ecological processes such as competition, predation or the effect of pesticides are evaluated in terms of change in population size. Population size, technically called population density (N), need not be measured in numbers only, and it keeps changing with food availability, predation and weather.

What is the difference in the method of measuring population density in an area if there are 200 carrot grass plants but only a single huge banyan tree?
questions.solution: Carrot grass can be measured by counting numbers, but for one huge banyan tree numbers are meaningless; percentage cover or biomass is used instead.

In nature, individuals of a species usually live in groups in a well-defined area, share or compete for similar resources, potentially interbreed and so form a population. A population has attributes that an individual does not, and is made up of individuals of different ages. Ecological processes such as competition, predation or the effect of pesticides are evaluated in terms of change in population size. Population size, technically called population density (N), need not be measured in numbers only, and it keeps changing with food availability, predation and weather.

Name two methods to measure the population density of tigers.
questions.solution: Counting pug marks and faecal pellets (camera traps are also used).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) What do you understand by 'MALT'? Where is it located in our body? (ii) Explain cytokine barriers. (iii) Name the diagnostic test for AIDS. On what principle does it work? (iv) Bone marrow and thymus play an important role in the human immune system. Explain how.
questions.solution: (i) Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue: lymphoid tissue in the lining of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts, about 50% of the body's lymphoid tissue. (ii) Virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection. (iii) ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay); it works on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction. (iv) They are primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow produces all blood cells including lymphocytes, and immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes there (B cells) or in the thymus (T cells).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Fill in H, I, J, K, L and M: (a) chemical: butyric acid, microorganism: H, category: I, use: important in food, chemical and pharma industry. (b) chemical: J, microorganism: Monascus purpureus, category: K, use: inhibits the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. (c) chemical: cyclosporin A, microorganism: L, category: fungus, use: M. (ii) Why are baculoviruses used as biological control agents?
questions.solution: (i) H = Clostridium butylicum; I = bacterium; J = statins; K = fungus (yeast); L = Trichoderma polysporum; M = immunosuppressive agent in organ transplant patients. (ii) Baculoviruses (genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus) attack insects and other arthropods; they are species-specific with narrow-spectrum action, do not harm non-target organisms such as plants, mammals and beneficial insects, and suit integrated pest management in ecologically sensitive areas.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Distinguish between the two cells enclosed in a mature male gametophyte of an angiosperm. (b) A diagram shows three modes of pollination: in method 1 pollen goes from the anther to the stigma of the same flower; in method 2 pollen goes between two flowers on the same plant; in method 3 pollen goes from a flower of one plant to a flower of another plant. (i) Write the technical terms for methods 1, 2 and 3. (ii) How do (a) water lily and (b) Vallisneria achieve pollination? (iii) Write the advantages of pollen transfer by method 3.
questions.solution: (a) The vegetative cell is larger, has abundant food reserve and a large irregular nucleus, and forms the pollen tube. The generative cell is small, spindle-shaped, floats in the vegetative cell's cytoplasm and divides to form two male gametes. (b)(i) 1: autogamy; 2: geitonogamy; 3: xenogamy (cross-pollination). (ii)(a) Water lily flowers rise above the water and are pollinated by insects or wind. (b) In Vallisneria, female flowers reach the water surface on long stalks, and male flowers or pollen released on the surface are carried passively by water currents to them. (iii) Xenogamy brings genetically different pollen, giving genetic variation and hybrid vigour, and avoids inbreeding depression.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Perform a cross between two sickle-cell carriers. What ratio is obtained between carrier, disease-free and diseased individuals in the F₁ progeny? Name the nitrogenous base substituted in the haemoglobin gene in this disease. (ii) Explain the difference in inheritance of flower colour in garden pea and snapdragon with the help of monohybrid crosses.
questions.solution: (i) HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ → 1 HbᴬHbᴬ (disease free) : 2 HbᴬHbˢ (carrier) : 1 HbˢHbˢ (diseased), i.e. carrier : disease free : diseased = 2 : 1 : 1. A single base change (GAG → GUG) substitutes adenine with thymine in the DNA (uracil in mRNA), so glutamic acid at the sixth position of the β-chain is replaced by valine. (ii) Pea shows complete dominance: RR (violet) × rr (white) gives all violet F₁; F₂ is 3 violet : 1 white (genotype 1:2:1). Snapdragon shows incomplete dominance: RR (red) × rr (white) gives pink F₁ (Rr); F₂ is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Explain with the help of well-labelled diagrams how the lac operon operates in E. coli : (i) in the presence of an inducer (ii) in the absence of an inducer.
questions.solution: The lac operon has a regulator gene i, a promoter p, an operator o and structural genes z (β-galactosidase), y (permease) and a (transacetylase). (ii) Without an inducer, the repressor made by the i gene binds to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase, so the structural genes are not transcribed. (i) When lactose (or allolactose, the inducer) is present, it binds the repressor, which changes shape and cannot bind the operator. RNA polymerase then transcribes z, y and a as one polycistronic mRNA, and the enzymes for lactose metabolism are made. This is negative regulation.
